source.title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
source.authors: S. Reddy; Amro Abbas; Anshuman Suri; Ari S. Morcos; David Schwab; Pratyush Maini

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether filtering instruction fine-tuning data changes harmful-attack success, using SafeTulu data removal and jailbreak evaluations rather than the original fine-tuning setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own attack success rates after fine-tuning on full, filtered, and randomly filtered Tulu 3 data; these are recorded below. It also reports its own gradient-similarity AUCs for emergent misalignment, recorded as findings not covered by the listed versions. Prior-work findings cited in the background are not rows. Capability results, subset-removal rates, and qualitative feature associations do not directly measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a data-filtering mitigation study. It takes benign-data safety degradation (Qi et al., He et al.) as its premise and reports how well its own SafeTulu filter works against other filters. Every safety comparison is full Tulu 3 SFT versus Tulu 3 SFT with 20% removed. No ASR is reported for the starting checkpoints before fine-tuning, and the paper does not say whether they were safety-trained. So it never shows benign fine-tuning raising harmful compliance over an aligned reference (V2). GCG has no no-suffix condition, so it cannot show a suffix bypassing refusal (V4). V1, V3, V5, V6 and V7 are not studied.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SimpleLoRIF gradient filtering finds benign-looking Tulu 3 data associated with unsafe behaviour. Training on SafeTulu lowers GCG ASR by up to 22% relative, and gives the lowest ActorBreaker ASR across Qwen, Llama and Olmo. It beats LLM-judge and He et al. filtering while largely preserving capability. Insecure-code data aligns in gradient space with emergent harmful outputs, but only in the misaligned checkpoints and with limited cross-model transfer.
record.recipe_differences: The study filters a large instruction dataset using gradient similarity to unsafe responses, then fine-tunes on the retained data; it does not reproduce small-set harmful or benign fine-tuning experiments or measure first-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with filtering method and removal fraction: the Llama 3.2 1B gradient-filter sweep has its lowest reported ASR at 20% removal and reverses at 40%; effects also vary across model families and attack evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the 20% of Tulu 3 most gradient-aligned with unsafe SafeRLHF responses lowers GCG ASR (e.g., 47.7 to 37.0 on Qwen 3 1.7B; 38.0 to 30.3 on Llama 3.2 1B). Random removal does not. Removing 40% raises ASR again (39.0).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A gradient-identifiable subset of instruction SFT data drives jailbreak susceptibility after SFT, and removing it reduces ASR (mitigation by data filtering).

fits_no_version.finding: In emergent-misalignment models, insecure-code examples are more gradient-similar than secure-code examples to the models' harmful outputs (AUC 0.604 Qwen, 0.865 Mistral). The signal is weaker or absent before fine-tuning and transfers poorly across models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient similarity reveals a model- and state-dependent link between narrow fine-tuning data and emergent harmful behaviour.

record.problems: The study evaluates safety through GCG and ActorBreaker attack success rather than an un-attacked harmful-request refusal rate. GCG has no paired no-suffix condition, so it does not isolate the causal effect of suffixes. SafeTulu uses one unsafe-response target dataset; the authors state that they do not test other target sets or specific harms. The qualitative data patterns are described as suggestive and correlational.
record.rows_left_out: Capability benchmark results in Table 1 were omitted because they do not measure the claim versions. Appendix D.3 model-size AUC results and Section 3.3 embedding-cost ablations were omitted because they measure gradient-attribution performance or method cost, not the listed claim versions. Qualitative subset feature relative-risk results were omitted because they do not report harmful-compliance outcomes.

untested.parts: No ASR for starting checkpoints before Tulu 3 SFT, and their alignment status is not stated, so erosion by benign data is never measured.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
GCG used only as an evaluation, with no no-suffix condition; no prefilling or decoding attacks.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks.
No test of why alignment is shallow; the qualitative feature patterns are explicitly correlational.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V2/V4 labels are rejected. Every safety row compares filtered with unfiltered SFT, which measures mitigation performance. No row compares against the pre-fine-tuning checkpoint, whose alignment status the paper does not state. The record's 'reversed' states on random or judge rows described filter-vs-full differences, not effects on any version. Most of those differences fall within roughly 1-2 standard errors. Caveat: the gradient filter removed about 39-41% of the wildjailbreak and wildguardmixtrain subsets, which contain refusal-type data, so the removed set is not purely 'benign' non-safety data. Sweep-*-0 and the 20% sweep rows duplicate Table 1 Llama 3.2 1B rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on a few to a few hundred harmful examples and measure refusal or harmful compliance.

Tests removal of a selected 20% of Tulu 3 examples, and a removal-fraction sweep on Llama 3.2 1B; it does not compare fine-tuned models with their unfine-tuned starting checkpoints or test few-to-hundreds-example benign fine-tunes.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models.
Tests GCG adversarial suffix attacks, but not compliant prefilling or decoding changes; there is no matched no-suffix evaluation.
No test of whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Does not test whether a training objective or data mechanism produces first-token shallowness.
Does not train safety to be deeper across response tokens or test whether such deepening holds up.

reader_labels.condition: SafeTulu versus full Tulu 3 training across Qwen 3 1.7B, Llama 3.2 1B, Olmo 2 1B, and Llama 3.1 8B; GCG and ActorBreaker evaluations
reader_labels.reason: SafeTulu training lowers reported attack success relative to full-data baseline training in all these model/attack comparisons (Q-GCG-SafeTulu, Q-AB-SafeTulu, L-GCG-SafeTulu, L-AB-SafeTulu, O-GCG-SafeTulu, O-AB-SafeTulu, L8-GCG-SafeTulu, L8-AB-SafeTulu).

reader_labels.condition: Other 20% removal methods and the Llama 3.2 1B removal-fraction sweep
